title: Bombay HC Holds an ICC's Threshold Rejection of a POSH Complaint Is Still Appealable Under Section 18
meta_description: Bombay High Court rules that even a summary dismissal for lacking a sexual element counts as a recommendation an aggrieved party can appeal.
case_name: Anup Vikal v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
citation: Writ Petition No. 7430 of 2026, decided 19 August 2026
body: An Internal Committee under the Prevention of Sexual Harassment Act is meant to make two kinds of decisions: whether a complaint even alleges conduct of a sexual nature, and, if it does, whether that conduct actually happened. The Bombay High Court has now held that an aggrieved party can appeal the first kind of decision too, even when the committee never reaches the second question at all.

The dispute arose out of three connected writ petitions filed by Anup Vikal, Chandrani Sen and Rohit Anand, whose complaints an Internal Complaints Committee had closed at the threshold, finding that the conduct complained of lacked any sexual element and therefore fell outside the committee's jurisdiction to examine on the merits. The complainants appealed that closure to the Industrial Court under Section 18 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, which by judgment dated 4 May 2026 rejected the respondents' objection that no appeal lay at all, set aside the ICC's communication, and remanded the matter for a fresh inquiry.

That maintainability question then travelled to the Bombay High Court on the respondents' writ petitions, which argued that Section 18 permits an appeal only against a 'recommendation' the ICC makes after inquiring into a complaint under Section 13, and that a threshold finding of no sexual element is not an inquiry outcome at all but a gatekeeping decision that falls outside appeal altogether. On this reading, a complainant whose grievance never crosses the sexual-element threshold would have no statutory route to challenge that screening decision, leaving the ICC's own view of what counts as sexual harassment effectively unreviewable by any appellate forum under the Act.

Justice Sandeep Marne rejected that reading. The judgment holds that any decision an ICC takes after considering a complaint, including a summary rejection for lacking a sexual element, qualifies as a recommendation within the meaning of Section 13(2) and is therefore appealable under Section 18. The existence of a complaint that genuinely alleges sexual harassment is, the Court accepted, a jurisdictional fact that conditions the ICC's power to proceed to a full inquiry, but a mistaken or contestable call on that jurisdictional fact is itself something the statute contemplates being tested on appeal rather than left to the ICC's own unreviewable judgment.

Having settled the maintainability question in the complainants' favour, the Court did not simply affirm the Industrial Court's order. It set aside that order to the extent it had gone on to decide the merits of whether the conduct actually involved a sexual element, holding that the Industrial Court should not have resolved that question itself at the appellate stage without the kind of fuller inquiry the ICC is meant to conduct in the first instance. The matter was remanded to the Industrial Court to decide the narrower question of jurisdictional fact afresh, leaving the substantive merits for a properly constituted ICC inquiry further down the line if the appeal succeeds.

For employers running Internal Committees, the practical effect is to remove whatever comfort came from treating a threshold dismissal as functionally final. A complainant who is told the conduct described does not amount to sexual harassment, and whose complaint is accordingly closed without any inquiry into the facts, retains a statutory right of appeal against that closure itself, which means the ICC's screening decisions carry the same exposure to appellate review as its findings after a full inquiry.

Employers and ICC members should accordingly treat even a threshold rejection as a decision requiring a reasoned basis capable of withstanding appellate scrutiny, rather than as an administrative filtering step outside the statute's reach. Workplaces that rely on quick, informal screening to dispose of complaints they consider borderline should expect that screening call to be tested on the same appellate standard as a full merits finding, not waved through as a preliminary matter beyond Section 18's scope. Internal policies that currently treat an ICC's threshold call as administratively final should be revised to build in reasons and a documented record before the complaint file is closed.
why_it_matters: Internal Committees can no longer treat a threshold finding that a complaint lacks a sexual element as a final, unreviewable screening decision; employers must now ensure even summary rejections rest on a reasoned jurisdictional assessment, since a complainant retains the statutory right under Section 18 to appeal that closure before any full inquiry into the underlying facts of the complaint ever takes place at all.
card_summary: Bombay HC rules an ICC's threshold rejection of a POSH complaint for lacking a sexual element is still a 'recommendation' appealable under Section 18, remanding the matter.
card_tip: Record a reasoned basis even for a threshold dismissal of a POSH complaint, since that screening decision is now appealable under Section 18 like a full inquiry finding.
verification_notes: The citation (Writ Petition No. 7430 of 2026), decision date (19 August 2026), the presiding judge (Justice Sandeep Marne), the three connected petitioners, the Industrial Court's 4 May 2026 order, the holding that a threshold ICC rejection counts as a Section 13(2) recommendation appealable under Section 18, and the remand confined to the jurisdictional-fact question are corroborated across Verdictum, Raw Law, LegalDeli and SupremeToday. One secondary source (Casemine) cites a later commentary date of 26 August 2026, which is a commentary date rather than the judgment date and is not relied on here.
